source: Verschueren, Schaeken & d'Ydewalle (2005) Everyday conditional reasoning: a working memory-dependent tradeoff between counterexample and likelihood use
finding: Founding paper of the dual-strategy idea. People who think aloud on everyday if-then problems use two kinds of information: counterexamples (cases that break the conclusion) or likelihood (how probable the conclusion is). Higher working-memory people use more counterexamples; lower ones use more likelihood. Strategy depends on capacity, not only performance.
numbers: 54 students (18 each in low, medium, high operation-span groups, picked from a pool of 292 tested with Gospan; group means 18.5, 32, 47.9). 1,728 think-aloud answers. Share of answers by type: counterexample 52.6%, bare acceptance 25.8%, likelihood 9.8% (F(2,50)=167.33). Counterexample use rose with span: low .472, medium .543, high .563 (linear trend F(1,51)=4.60, p<.05). Likelihood use fell: .143, .084, .067 (F(1,51)=8.01). Acceptance rate did not vary with span.
quote: Participants with lower working memory capacity more often use probabilistic information
limits: Small sample. Verbal reports can change the thinking they report. Counterexample share rose only about 9 points from low to high span. Span-by-answer-type interaction was only marginal (p=.055). Content is everyday causal conditionals, not abstract logic. About 12% of AC and 23% of MP codes had to be re-rated by the two raters.
agent_relevance: Strategy choice depends on available capacity: a cheap likelihood route for low capacity, an expensive counterexample search for high capacity. For a small model with a short budget, expect the cheap route to dominate unless the scaffold forces the search.

source: Markovits (2024) Are There Two Kinds of Reasoners? (section 1: the diagnostic instrument)
finding: The key measurement tool. Abstract affirmation-of-consequent problems (If P then Q; Q is true; is P true?) on a made-up planet come with counts from 1,000 observations. Ten problems: five with about 90% P-and-Q cases, five with about 50%. A counterexample reasoner rejects all ten (any not-P-and-Q case is a counterexample). A statistical reasoner rejects the 50% problems more than the 90% ones, tracking the probability. Three modus ponens fillers are added.
numbers: Coding rule: R50 = rejections out of 5 for the 50% items, R90 for the 90% items. R50 > R90+1 gives Statistical; R90+R50 = 10 gives Counterexample; R90 = 4 gives Intermediate; anything else is Other. Original instrument had 13 items (5 at about 10% alternative antecedents, 5 at about 50%, 3 at 0%). Only about two thirds of people fall in the two main groups.
quote: A reasoner who focused on potential counterexamples would reject all of these inferences.
limits: The test is one item type (AC with explicit frequencies). A single item would not be diagnostic, because there is no rule to turn a probability into a yes/no. A risk that the test only sorts people who apply formal logic from those who do not was checked; see a03.
agent_relevance: A strategy can be detected from how a response changes with explicit probability: if the verdict ignores the stated odds it is counterexample-like, if it follows the odds it is statistical-like. We can run the same probe on a model.

source: Markovits (2024) Are There Two Kinds of Reasoners? (sections 1 to 2: logical-form control and capacity)
finding: Counterexample reasoners are not just 'more logical'. On modus ponens (valid) paired with potential counterexamples, they endorse the valid conclusion LESS often than statistical reasoners (Markovits et al. 2016, reported in the review, not opened). Counterexample reasoners do have higher IQ, CRT and open-mindedness scores, but strategy predicts performance over and above them.
numbers: Composite z-score of IQ, CRT and actively open-minded thinking: Counterexample M = 0.438, Statistical M = -0.099 (Markovits 2024). Thompson & Markovits (2021): strategy explained variance in belief bias, base-rate neglect and denominator neglect beyond IQ, CRT and numeracy. Intermediate group has capacity between the two; Other group is lowest.
limits: Secondhand for the 2016, 2021 and 2024 originals. The review is by the model's main author, so it may present the model favourably.
agent_relevance: A search for counterexamples can wrongly reject a valid conclusion when a fake counterexample is easy to imagine. A counterexample step needs a check that the counterexample actually fits the stated premises.

source: Markovits (2024) Are There Two Kinds of Reasoners? (sections 5 to 6: time pressure, switching, confidence)
finding: Under time pressure people shift toward the statistical pattern; the statistical strategy is the default under steep constraint. People who start with unlimited time and then get a deadline mostly keep a counterexample pattern, and some statistical reasoners move to counterexample. The size of a later switch is predicted by confidence in the first strategy. This is evidence of some metacognitive control.
numbers: Markovits et al. (2013), reported in the review (original not opened): a time-constrained group gave many more statistical patterns than an unlimited-time group; confidence in a strategy predicted keeping it later. Markovits (2024): first block of belief-bias problems with unlimited time, then a 4 s block; correct responses dropped only for Counterexample reasoners (less so for Intermediate); Statistical and Other showed almost no change.
limits: The review text says in one place that counterexample responding was 'significantly faster' in the 2013 study. This contradicts every other statement in the same paper and the 2017 and 2020 data (counterexample slower), so it is probably a slip; we treat counterexample as slower. The 2013 original was not opened.
agent_relevance: A deadline or a small token budget is a strategy switch, not just noise: it moves a reasoner from search to estimate. Our budget rules (G11, G12) should decide the strategy on purpose rather than letting short budgets do it silently.

source: Markovits (2024) Are There Two Kinds of Reasoners? (section 6: can strategy be changed on purpose)
finding: Strategy can be changed by short instruction, but unevenly. Markovits & Thompson (2023): training to reason by counterexample or by probability. How well people followed the instruction depended on their starting strategy. Statistical reasoners who followed the instruction changed their later answers; Counterexample reasoners changed little.
numbers: Ability to follow counterexample instructions declined linearly across Counterexample, Intermediate, Statistical, Other. Follow-up tasks: Study 1 belief-biased syllogisms, Study 2 base-rate problems. No sample sizes in the review. Review conclusion: strategy is 'relatively stable in the short term' but 'not invariant'.
limits: Only the review was opened; the 2023 paper itself was not. Direction of change differed between belief-bias and base-rate tasks. Durability of the change was not shown.
agent_relevance: Support for a scaffold that tells the model which route to use per item class: the statistical-leaning reasoner is the one an instruction moves most. For models, test whether instruction shifts a weak model more than a strong one.

source: Markovits (2024) Are There Two Kinds of Reasoners? (sections 7 to 9: Intermediate, Other, children)
finding: A richer split than two types. Intermediate: counterexample users who sometimes default to statistical (rejects 4 of the five 90% items). Other: probably people who did not understand the diagnostic items. Children as young as 6 show both kinds of reasoning; counterexample use grows from 6 to 9 while probabilistic judgement stays flat; under a time limit both fall in parallel in 8 and 10 year olds.
numbers: Intermediate group capacity lies between Counterexample and Statistical on IQ, CRT, AOT; Other is lower than Statistical. About two thirds of participants are classifiable into the two main groups.
limits: Developmental findings are from older studies (Markovits & Thompson 2008; Markovits et al. 2019), not opened. The link from children's data to adult strategies is speculation, in the author's words.
agent_relevance: Strategy use is graded and tied to ability, so a weak model may behave like an Intermediate or Other type: it lapses back to estimation even when told to search.

source: Markovits, Brisson, de Chantal & Thompson (2017) Interactions between inferential strategies and belief bias
finding: Statistical reasoners are more swayed by whether a conclusion sounds true. Three studies on invalid, valid and 'Most' syllogisms, each with the strategy diagnostic. Counterexample reasoners accepted fewer conclusions overall and showed a smaller believability gap. Both groups noticed the clash between belief and validity (same response-time and confidence pattern).
numbers: Study 1 (invalid 'All A are B' forms; N=170 analysed: 87 counterexample, 83 statistical): believable-conclusion acceptance out of 4: CE 1.71 vs statistical 3.01; unbelievable: 0.24 vs 0.54. Belief effect 1.47 (CE, d=1.04) vs 2.47 (stat, d=1.66); strategy by type interaction F(1,168)=19.92, partial eta2=.106. Study 2 (valid modus tollens, N=189): belief effect 1.38 (stat, d=.80) vs 0.25 (CE, not significant, t(78)=1.28); CE slower (24.81 s vs 19.92 s, F(1,153)=10.05). Study 3 ('Most' syllogisms, N=121): belief effect 1.96 (stat) vs 1.21 (CE), interaction F(1,99)=7.23, partial eta2=.068.
quote: reasoners using a statistical strategy were more prone to the effects of conclusion belief across all three forms of reasoning
limits: Students only, French-speaking. Reasoners fitting neither pattern ('Other') were dropped: the Study 1 table lists 61 Other plus 170 classified, a total of 231, while the text says N=170, so the text N counts analysed people only. Strategy order shifted category counts slightly (statistical was more common when belief problems came first, not significant). Belief bias shrank but was not removed in counterexample reasoners in Studies 1 and 3.
agent_relevance: The belief-bias gap is a strategy effect: the estimate route mixes in 'does this sound true?'. Our S1 content-swap and isolation of the logical core matter most when the model is on the estimate route.

source: de Chantal, Newman, Thompson & Markovits (2020) Who resists belief-biased inferences? Reasoning strategies, working memory, and attentional focus
finding: Strategy predicts resistance to belief bias beyond working memory, and eye tracking shows why: on belief-versus-logic conflict items counterexample reasoners look longer at the premises, while looking time at the conclusion does not differ by strategy.
numbers: Study 1 (N=139; classified 62 statistical = 45%, 43 counterexample = 31%, 34 other = 24%; 66 kept after working-memory exclusions): strategy beta = -.42, p<.001; working memory beta = -.21, p=.07; together 27.7% of variance in belief score. Working memory alone 10.9%; strategy added 15.5%; strategy alone 23.7%. Statistical reasoners answered faster (6.36 s vs 8.84 s). Study 2 (N=196, eye tracking; 113 classified: 74 statistical, 39 counterexample): conflict-item accuracy .42 overall; counterexample better, Welch t(61.0)=4.6, d=1.0; neutral items no difference (d=.3). Counterexample reasoners fixated premises longer on conflict items (d=.57). Counterexample reasoners made no errors on no-conflict items. Confidence did not differ by strategy.
limits: Study 1 analysis used only 47.5% of the sample after pre-set exclusions (the authors also ran a continuous-score check on all 139). About 35% of the Study 2 sample was unclassifiable. Correlational, so strategy could be a marker of something else. The 2024 review says statistical reasoners looked more at the conclusion; this paper found no such difference, only less premise time.
agent_relevance: A concrete process signature for 'search' versus 'estimate': time and attention spent on premises when belief and logic clash. For a model, a similar signature could be how much of the answer cites the premises versus the conclusion's plausibility.

source: Markovits, de Chantal, Brisson, Dube, Thompson & Newman (2021) Reasoning strategies predict use of very fast logical reasoning
finding: Under very short deadlines strategy predicts accuracy and working memory stops predicting it. Counterexample reasoners could still spot non sequiturs and reject invalid AC at 3.5 s; statistical reasoners fell to chance on non sequiturs at 3.5 s.
numbers: Study 1 (N=206, online; 3.5 s group 44 CE, 32 stat, 25 other; 5 s group 41 CE, 30 stat, 34 other): non sequitur rejection 3.5 s .66 vs 5 s .82; statistical .60 vs CE .84 (strategy F(1,143)=21.67, partial eta2=.132); statistical at 3.5 s .503 (chance), CE at 3.5 s .76. AC correct rejection CE .59 vs stat .31 (AA .94, AC .45 overall). Study 2 (N=291; 149 at 4 s, 142 unlimited; 15.2% of 4 s trials unanswered): in the 4 s group strategy predicted rejection of non sequiturs (b=.07, p=.046) and AC (b=.32, p<.001) while working memory had no effect (t<1); with unlimited time both predicted. Models explained 33.6% and 42.6% of variance. Study 3 per its abstract: strategy explained fast belief-biased responding over and above IQ (not read in detail).
limits: Online sample paid about 2 pounds; timing accuracy is limited. Working memory and strategy correlate only r=.12 here. 'Other' dropped. The claim that capacity is a very poor predictor under severe time pressure rests on non-significant regression terms.
agent_relevance: Fast logical answers are not free for everyone: some reasoners carry a premise-focused habit that works at speed. A model's quick first pass may be good or bad depending on that habit, so measure first-pass quality per item class instead of assuming it.

source: Markovits, Brisson & de Chantal (2015) Additional evidence for a dual-strategy model of reasoning: probabilistic reasoning is more invariant than reasoning about logical validity
finding: Same stated odds, two different questions. When asked 'is the conclusion logically valid?', strategy changes how people react to new evidence: counterexample reasoners barely rise after being told the conclusion is very likely, statistical reasoners do. When asked 'how probable is it?', both groups answer the same. So the strategy difference lives in turning a probability into a yes/no validity verdict.
numbers: Study 1 (N=107: 53 CE, 30 stat, 24 other): AC and DA acceptance (of 2) before update: 1.51, 1.50, 1.33; after update: CE 0.13, stat 0.97, other 0.71. Strategy by inference interaction F(1,74)=15.29, partial eta2=.171. Study 2 (N=86): probability ratings CE .789 to .775, stat .763 to .762, no strategy effect (power 99.9% for the Study 1 effect size). Study 3 (N=92): doing probability ratings first reduced the later validity drop (validity acceptance 1.33 to 0.96) compared with validity first (1.40 to 0.53); probability ratings were unchanged by order (.803 to .795).
limits: French-speaking students, paper booklets. Updating effect rests on very few items (two inferences per person). Authors note updated probability estimates barely rise even with strong evidence. The data do not tie the counterexample strategy to mental models; the authors say it could fit a probabilistic account.
agent_relevance: The question format picks the strategy. Asking a model for a probability may produce the cheap route; asking 'does it necessarily follow?' invites the search. A scaffold can pick the route by changing the output question.

source: Brisson & Markovits (2020) Reasoning strategies and semantic memory effects in deductive reasoning
finding: Strategy shows up only on the uncertain inferences (AC and DA), not on the certain ones (MP, MT), and only when the question is about logical validity. With explicit probability instructions the strategy gap disappears. So both groups retrieve the same stored alternatives; they differ in how they turn them into a yes/no.
numbers: Study 1 (N=104: 47 CE, 38 stat, 19 other): more alternatives lowered endorsement of invalid inferences (1.73 with few vs 0.81 with many, out of 3) but little for valid ones (2.61 vs 2.12); premise-type effect F(1,77)=16.42, partial eta2=.176. Study 2 (incompatibility statements, N=212: 117 CE, 65 stat, 30 other) replicated. Study 3 (likelihood instructions, N=157: 86 CE, 39 stat): valid conclusions rated 83.5, invalid 61.8; counterexample reasoners gave higher estimates overall (77.0 vs 68.3) but the validity-by-strategy interaction was absent (F(1,115)=1.45, p=.23), unlike earlier studies.
limits: Only alternative antecedents were varied, not disabling conditions; the authors call that a gap. Not preregistered; data not archived. 'Other' reasoners dropped.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that the retrieval step is shared and the decision threshold is the strategy. For an agent: list alternatives first (shared), then apply an explicit rule for what counts as reject (a policy we can set).

source: Markovits, Lortie Forgues & Brunet (2010) Conditional reasoning, frequency of counterexamples, and the effect of response modality
finding: Early demonstration that the answer format changes the processing mode. With a scaled certainty rating people track exception frequency, replicating Geiger and Oberauer. With a yes/no 'does it follow logically' answer the profile is different: any exception rejects the conclusion.
numbers: Study 1 (N=138): categorical condition accepted the conclusion 87.1% of the time with no exceptions, with no reliable differences among the other four problem types; scaled condition replicated the frequency effect. Study 2 (N=172): in the categorical condition higher-competence reasoners (49 people above the median of 4 of 8 on abstract problems) accepted fewer 10%-exception modus ponens inferences (.23 vs .54) and 50%-exception ones (.00 vs .12); no competence difference with scaled answers.
limits: Pre-dates the diagnostic; strategy was not measured directly. Paper-and-pencil, student samples. A median split on abstract competence is arbitrary.
agent_relevance: Same input, different mode depending on response scale. A scaffold asking for a grade of belief gets statistical behaviour; one asking for a necessary yes/no gets search behaviour.

source: Geiger & Oberauer (2007) Reasoning with conditionals: Does every counterexample count? It's frequency that counts
finding: Probabilistic side of the argument. People's belief in an if-then rule and their willingness to infer from it follow the frequency of exceptions, not the number of different disabling conditions behind them. Disabling conditions matter only when no frequency is given.
numbers: Experiment 1 (N=27, psychology students): frequency of exceptions affected the rating of the conditional (F(1,26)=23.1, partial eta2=.47) and modus ponens (F(1,26)=34.0, partial eta2=.50); the number of disabling conditions had no effect. Experiment 2 replicated. Experiment 3 (no frequency info; df implies about 20 to 22 people): number of disablers lowered belief, F(1,19)=35.2, partial eta2=.63. Experiment 4 extended to everyday conditionals (about 30 people).
limits: Rating-scale answers, which Markovits et al. (2010) argue push people into the probabilistic mode. Small within-subject samples. One effect (exceptions on modus tollens) did not replicate between Experiments 1 and 2, and the authors have no explanation.
agent_relevance: Shows what the statistical route weighs: how often exceptions happen, not how many kinds. A model on this route will under-weight a single sharp counterexample.

source: Beeson, Stupple, Schofield & Staples (2019) Mental Models or Probabilistic Reasoning or Both: Reviewing the Evidence for and Implications of Dual-Strategy Models of Deductive Reasoning
finding: The review our catalogue cites as 'Beeson et al. 2019' is a theory review with no new experiments, written by a Derby group, not Markovits. It proposes Mental Models Theory and the Probability Heuristics Model as the candidate formal specifications of the two strategies, ties the model to dual-process, dual-source and meta-reasoning accounts, and lists hypotheses.
numbers: No new data. Key proposals: (1) syllogism figure should hurt a counterexample strategy (non-contiguous middle terms need premise reordering) but not a statistical one; (2) strategy selection is a meta-reasoning decision, probably picking the least demanding strategy (Beilock and DeCaro, 2007); (3) statistical reasoners may be failing to decouple belief from the problem; (4) whether the preference is a continuum or two types is open.
limits: Proposals, not tests. The authors call the highly specified MMT and PHM pair 'double-edged': strong predictions but less parsimony. They also note counterexample users who never go past a first model may be dichotomous thinkers rather than searchers.
agent_relevance: A clean test for our agent: syllogism figure as a load probe for the search route. Also suggests strategy choice is itself a monitored decision (confidence, cost), which fits a code-controlled gate.

source: Beeson et al. (2019), second reading: the statistical strategy as PHM, and the switching question
finding: The statistical strategy is specified as the Probability Heuristics Model: heuristics produce a probably-valid conclusion fast, and a test (the max-heuristic confidence) estimates how likely it is. 'No valid conclusion' answers are a known weak spot of PHM, but a counterexample strategy predicts them. So the pair can explain more than either alone. Whether people switch strategy by item or by task is not settled.
numbers: Cites Roberts (2000): people can change strategy between tasks or even trials. Hattori (2016) and Elflein & Ragni (2018) are cited for criticisms of PHM conclusions (not opened). Two-response method on PHM: min-conclusions got stronger feeling of rightness and were reassessed less (cited, not opened).
limits: The review says PHM may describe 'a possible strategy rather than a fundamental reasoning mechanism', the same move the dual-strategy model makes. Many tests it cites are secondhand here.
agent_relevance: Gives an item-class rule for the agent: use the min-heuristic style estimate where an informative answer is cheap and checkable, and force the counterexample search where the question asks about necessity or 'nothing follows'.

source: Chater & Oaksford (1999) The Probability Heuristics Model of Syllogistic Reasoning (the model)
finding: The formal statistical-side model. Quantified statements are ordered by informativeness. Three generation heuristics: min (take the quantifier of the LEAST informative premise as the conclusion), p-entailment (the next preferred conclusion is the one probabilistically implied by the min-conclusion), attachment (the subject of the conclusion follows the min-premise's end term). One test heuristic: max (confidence in a conclusion depends on how informative the MOST informative premise is). People do not compute probabilistic validity; the heuristics converge on it.
numbers: Informativeness is defined by information theory; a 'rarity' assumption (properties apply to few objects) fixes the order. For the standard AIEO quantifiers, the min-heuristic conclusion type matches the p-valid conclusion in 22 of 31 p-valid syllogisms; adding Most and Few, 32 of 38 match (all six violations are O conclusions).
limits: The probabilistic validity derivation is only referenced; the authors offered the maths on request. PHM has trouble with 'no valid conclusion' answers (Hattori 2016, via Beeson et al.). Fits are to older data sets.
agent_relevance: A cheap, rule-like procedure we can implement in code: given two quantified premises, predict the heuristic answer, and flag where the logically valid answer differs from it. Those disagreement items are where a search is worth paying for.

source: Chater & Oaksford (1999) The Probability Heuristics Model of Syllogistic Reasoning (the meta-analysis and its fit)
finding: The min-heuristic explains most human syllogism answers, including wrong ones. In a meta-analysis of five studies on all 64 syllogisms the model fits closely, and only about half of answers are logically correct. Logic plays a small residual role beyond the heuristics.
numbers: Studies: Dickstein 1978 (N=22 and N=76), Johnson-Laird & Steedman 1978 (N=20, N=20), Johnson-Laird & Bara 1984 (N=20). Fit over 320 data points: r(318)=.90, root-mean-square deviation .30 (over 80% of variance). Max-premise parameters: A 70.14%, I 31.11%, E 18.78%, O 18.04% of choices by the min-heuristic; p-entailment about 10.76%, error 1.22%. On invalid syllogisms alone the min-heuristic predicts 95.17% of conclusions drawn (excluding no-valid-conclusion); fit r(208)=.90. Logically correct answers 51.8% overall and 64.9% on valid syllogisms (chance 20% forced-choice, 11.1% production).
limits: The meta-analysis pools earlier lab data from small samples. The model has about six fitted parameters. Dickstein's forced-choice task cuts the number of valid syllogisms from 27 to 19.
agent_relevance: Baseline for what a cheap heuristic can do: about 50% logically correct but systematic. An LLM's quick pass on syllogisms may look like this (see a23).

source: Chater & Oaksford (1999) The Probability Heuristics Model of Syllogistic Reasoning (new experiments with Most and Few)
finding: Novel predictions tested with generalised quantifiers, where logic and mental-model theories give no answer. The min-heuristic predicts the modal answer, and p-entailment conclusions appear as the second choice. Fit is good with the AMFO quantifiers and weaker with MFIE.
numbers: Experiment 1 (AMFO quantifiers): pmin 67.03%, pent1 38.93, pent2 17.01, perror 5.27; fit on p-invalid syllogisms r(102)=.92, rms .18. Experiment 2 (MFIE): r(254)=.65 (42% of variance), rms .26; parameters pmin 37.03, pent1 16.00, pent2 14.13, perror 12.28. For comparison, Rips (1994) reported r(254)=.74 with ten parameters on his own data.
limits: Fit is weaker where informativeness values are in the middle range, and the authors flag it. Samples are modest (a within-participant ANOVA with df 57 in Experiment 1).
agent_relevance: The statistical route extends to quantifiers a logic engine cannot score, so for 'most/few' items a code-side probability check is the only available grader.

source: Begin & Markovits (2022) Reasoning strategies and prior knowledge effects in contingency learning
finding: Strategy generalises outside deduction. In judging whether a cause produces an effect from tables of cases, counterexample reasoners give lower causal ratings than statistical reasoners, independently of how plausible the cause is and of the contingency.
numbers: Study 1 (N=200 online): strategy effect F(1,124)=4.61, p=.034, partial eta2=.036; plausibility F=14.77, partial eta2=.106. Study 2 (N=452: 181 statistical, 125 counterexample, 146 other): strategy F(1,298)=11.84, partial eta2=.038; Bayesian ANOVA inclusion factor 20.37 for strategy. Study 3 (active task) also reported strategy effects.
limits: Small effects (partial eta2 about .04). About a third of Study 2 participants were unclassifiable. The answer is a causal judgement scale, not logical validity.
agent_relevance: The 'weights disconfirming cases more' habit is a general property of the search route, so it may carry to an agent's evidence-weighing rules, such as how much one failing test should count.

source: Gratton & Markovits (2021) Reasoning strategies determine the effect of disconfirmation on belief in false claims
finding: A single disconfirming statement lowers belief much more in counterexample reasoners. Repetition of the claim's gist raises belief equally in both groups.
numbers: N=2,122 adults online (768 counterexample = 36.2%, 794 statistical = 37.4%, 560 other = 26.4%). Belief in the false claim (scale -7 to +7) after repetition: CE 3.81 vs stat 4.25 (not significant). After a single disconfirmation: CE 0.14 vs stat 1.75 (significant). Overall repetition M=4.04 vs disconfirmation M=0.95. Statistical overall belief higher: 3.00 vs 1.99.
limits: Online, one false-claim paradigm with two contents (Hylophobia 2.98 vs Phantosmia 2.02 mean belief, so content matters). There is no single normative answer, so the authors cannot say who is right.
agent_relevance: A disconfirming test should have a strong effect on the search route and a weak one on the estimate route. G2 says revise from real failing output; this says the effect of a single failing case depends on the mode, so code, not the model, should decide how much one failure counts.

source: Knauff & Gazzo Castaneda (2025) Reasoning beyond clicks: Disentangling counterexamples and probabilities in conditional reasoning
finding: A challenge to probabilistic accounts, and a warning about method. When people write free-text answers instead of clicking on a scale, about a third give a certain answer, and uncertainty is more often explained with a concrete counterexample than in probability words. The authors call it 'probabilistic masking': rating scales induce probabilistic responses.
numbers: Experiment 1: N=20; 29.6% of responses certain, 41.9% uncertain with counterexamples, rest probability words. Experiment 2: N=37; about one third certain, about 23% probabilistic, nearly half counterexample-based. Over 1,300 written responses in total. Certain answers were more common with high conditional probability (45.3% vs 13.9% low in Experiment 1; Wilcoxon z=5.16 in Experiment 2). Counterexample responses beat probability responses (z=2.94, p=.003, Experiment 2). Only two participants gave numerical estimates.
quote: what appears as probabilistic reasoning may often be a product of the measurement tool itself
limits: Small samples; coding categories were set by the authors, who suspect they undercounted counterexample reasoning (hedge words coded as probabilistic). Post-hoc written explanations are not process data. Nothing here uses the Markovits diagnostic.
agent_relevance: Supports the view that the answer format drives the strategy. For us: do not conclude a model reasons probabilistically from graded outputs; the scale may have made it so.

source: Kosourikhina & Handley (2025) Conflict detection with invalid inferences: All heuristics, no logic
finding: Boundary condition for the 'counterexample strategy is natural' story. Under speed, invalid AC and DA syllogisms feel valid to many people: they endorse them nearly as often as valid ones, and the conflict seen is between two heuristic answers, not logic versus heuristic.
numbers: Two experiments, total N=248. Speeded abstract items (7 s in Experiment 1): conclusion endorsed on 73% of valid items and 66% of invalid items (difference p=.06). Experiment 2: 63% of valid, 62% of invalid (p=.7). 'Reverse' conflict-detection effects on invalid items disappear when invalid items are scored as valid by the participant's own answer.
limits: Not a dual-strategy study; it does not measure strategy. Speeded items only. Shows fast responses are not logic-sensitive for these forms.
agent_relevance: A fast first pass on 'invalid but plausible' forms should be assumed wrong about half the time; verification must test the invalid forms specifically.

source: Bertolazzi, Gatt & Bernardi (2024) A Systematic Analysis of Large Language Models as Soft Reasoners: The Case of Syllogistic Inferences
finding: Language models show the 'estimate' signature on syllogisms. LLaMA-3 8B with zero-shot chain-of-thought rarely says 'nothing follows' (the invalid case), and its answers follow the old atmosphere heuristic. Fine-tuning helps valid inferences and removes most biases; in-context examples help valid inferences but increase contradictions.
numbers: Atmosphere theory predicts 92% of the correct valid conclusions of LLaMA-3 8B zero-shot CoT, and 82.97% of its errors on invalid and 62.79% on valid schemas. Contradictory answers: LLaMA-3 1.09%, Pythia 1.4B 18.91%; SFT Pythia 73.91% (70.47% from 'nothing follows' plus another conclusion). Heuristic coverage of ground truth: PHM predicts 60.42% of correct conclusions on valid syllogisms and 0% on invalid ones (no-valid-conclusion is not covered).
limits: Small models (Pythia 1.4B, LLaMA-3 8B), not frontier models. Atmosphere is the best fit but the authors cannot rule out other pattern matching. PHM is checked only as a coverage table.
agent_relevance: Models default to a heuristic answer and rarely claim 'nothing follows'. The scaffold needs an explicit counterexample step for the 'no valid conclusion' class, scored in code.

source: Verschueren, Schaeken & d'Ydewalle (2005) A dual-process specification of causal conditional reasoning (Thinking & Reasoning 11, 239-278)
finding: Companion founding paper, described by later papers (not opened here). Proposes that causal conditional inferences are made either by retrieving counterexamples (analytic, working-memory heavy, yes/no judgement) or by estimating likelihood (heuristic, quick). Verbal protocols showed both kinds, and counterexample access was slower than likelihood.
numbers: As summarised in Markovits (2024) and Beeson et al. (2019): think-aloud data; likelihood use more common with lower working-memory span; counterexample access slower. No numbers verified from this paper.
limits: Not opened. Numbers for the same design are in a01. Both Leuven papers used think-aloud reports, which may change the thinking.
agent_relevance: The origin of 'two strategies' as one person's two options, selected by capacity, rather than two kinds of people.

source: Markovits, Brunet, Thompson & Brisson (2013) time-pressure study of the strategy diagnostic (as reported by Markovits 2024, Markovits et al. 2015, Beeson et al. 2019)
finding: Original evidence that the two strategies are open to the same person. With a deadline most people give the statistical pattern; with unlimited time more give the counterexample pattern; confidence in the first strategy predicts keeping it.
numbers: No numbers verified (original not opened). Review-level facts: strategy diagnostic given with and without time constraint, confidence asked after.
limits: Original article not reached this session (paywall). Three secondary sources agree on direction. One secondary text states the opposite on response speed (see a04).
agent_relevance: The deadline-to-estimate shift is the main reason to set strategy by item class and not leave it to budget chance.

source: Markovits, Lortie Forgues & Brunet (2012) the first strategy diagnostic (as reported in Markovits et al. 2017, Markovits 2024)
finding: First use of the 13-item diagnostic with frequency information on the planet Kronus; counterexample reasoners did better on abstract reasoning tasks.
numbers: No numbers verified (original not opened). 13 items: 5 at 8-10%, 5 at 48-50%, 3 at 0% alternative-antecedent frequency, each out of 1,000 observations.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: The probe format can be copied for LLM tests with exact numbers.

source: Thompson & Markovits (2021) Reasoning strategy vs cognitive capacity as predictors of individual differences in reasoning performance
finding: Strategy explained variance in belief bias, base-rate neglect and denominator neglect over IQ, CRT and numeracy (per the description in Markovits 2024).
numbers: No numbers verified from the original (Cognition, paywalled; abstract not reached by search).
limits: Not opened; only a one-paragraph description in the 2024 review was read.
agent_relevance: Strategy predicts judgement-under-uncertainty errors beyond deduction, so a strategy probe may also help on estimation tasks.

source: Markovits & Thompson (2023) Can we change how people reason? Effects of instructions to reason differently and reasoning strategy (J Exp Psychol LMC 49, 1773-1785)
finding: Instruction-based change of strategy (summary only; see a05 for the review's account).
numbers: Citation confirmed by web search. Findings known only from the 2024 review.
limits: Not opened. Link points to the review that describes it.
agent_relevance: Test: does a 'search for a counterexample first' instruction move a weak model more than a strong one?
